instruction.text: Sometimes it can be difficult to tell who a pronoun is referring to. Is this sentence clear or unclear?

end.text: In this example, 'she' could refer to either Clara or her grandmother. This makes the meaning unclear. Try to avoid using pronouns when they could refer to more than one subject.

atoms.a: Clara saw her grandmother when she was crossing the road.

instruction.text: Select the sentence below that describes the situation more clearly.

b: ++While Clara was crossing the road, she saw her grandmother.
While she was crossing the road, Clara saw her grandmother.
Clara saw her grandmother while she crossed the road.

instruction.text: Is this sentence clear or unclear?

trainers.hint: Could the pronoun be referring to more than one subject?

atoms.a: Henry lost sight of his dad when he went into the shopping centre.

instruction.text: Select the sentence below that describes the situation more clearly.

b: ++When his dad went into the shopping centre, Henry lost sight of him.
When he went into the shopping centre, Henry lost sight of his dad.
Henry lost sight of his dad while he went inside the shopping centre.

instruction.text: Is this sentence clear or unclear?

trainers.hint: Could the pronoun be referring to more than one subject?

atoms.a: While Daisy was on the phone, she heard Emma nearby.

instruction.text: What do the blue pronouns in the sentence below refer to?

atoms.a: Lily and Martin argue a lot. <t-blue>She</t-blue> doesn’t like <t-blue>him</t-blue>.
The children have a lot of work to do. <t-blue>It</t-blue> is making <t-blue>them</t-blue> stressed.
Alex’s dad came to pick Alex up from school. <t-blue>He</t-blue> is waiting for <t-blue>him</t-blue> in the car.
